title: The Good, the Bad & the Ugly Behind the Desire for Promotion
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article sorts the motivations behind seeking promotion into three categories: good (a genuine desire to advance the organization), bad (compensation, status, or besting former peers), and an especially self-destructive "ugly" category -- accepting promotion purely out of guilt or obligation, believing the organization will fail without them. The author warns this obligation-driven motivation often leads to long-term stress and ineffectiveness, and closes with a T.S. Eliot line about doing the right deed for the wrong reason to argue that organizations should scrutinize why leaders want to advance before promoting them.
points: Motivations for seeking promotion are sorted into good, bad, and self-destructively "ugly" categories.
Good motivations center on a genuine desire to advance the organization through more influence.
Bad motivations include compensation, status, and outdoing former peers.
The ugliest motivation is a guilt-driven sense of obligation, which is linked to long-term stress and ineffectiveness.
quotes: The desire for the next role and a deserved promotion to a more senior leadership position seems to be a natural motivation in organizational life.
Not everyone who accepts an elevated role does so with positive intentions.
People who covet promotion solely for more compensation or for status make for ineffectual leaders.
The ugliest justification for promotion isn’t as bad as it is self-destructive.
As the poet T.S. Eliot so aptly noted, the greatest treason is “To do the right deed for the wrong reason.
